title: No. 30 — Concerning the General Power of Taxation (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I have already observed that the federal government ought to have the power to provide for the support of the national forces. By that proposition I meant to include the cost of raising troops, of building and equipping fleets, and all other expenses connected in any way with military arrangements and operations. But these are not the only objects for which the Union must necessarily be empowered to raise revenue. Its power must also cover the support of the national civil list, the payment of the national debts already contracted or yet to be contracted, and, in general, all those matters that will call for payments out of the national treasury. The conclusion is that a general power of taxation, in one form or another, must be built into the structure of the government.

Money is rightly considered the vital principle of the body politic: it is what sustains the body's life and motion and enables it to perform its most essential functions. A complete power to procure a regular and adequate supply of money, as far as the resources of the community will permit, may therefore be regarded as an indispensable ingredient of every constitution. Where this power is lacking, one of two evils must follow. Either the people must be subjected to continual plunder, as a substitute for a better way of supplying the public wants, or the government must waste away into a fatal atrophy and, in a short time, perish.

In the Ottoman or Turkish empire, the sovereign is in other respects the absolute master of the lives and fortunes of his subjects, yet he has no right to impose a new tax. The consequence is that he permits the pashas, or governors of provinces, to pillage the people without mercy, and then in turn squeezes out of them the sums he needs to meet his own necessities and those of the state. In America, from a like cause, the government of the Union has gradually dwindled into a state of decay that comes close to annihilation. Who can doubt that the happiness of the people in both countries would be advanced if competent authorities, placed in the proper hands, could provide the revenues that the public's necessities might require?

The present Confederation, feeble as it is, was intended to place in the United States an unlimited power to provide for the money needs of the Union. But because it proceeded on an erroneous principle, the power was set up in such a manner as entirely to defeat the intention. Under the articles that make up that compact (as I have already stated), Congress is authorized to determine and call for any sums of money that, in its judgment, are necessary for the service of the United States; and its requisitions, the formal requests it makes to the States for money, are, if they follow the rule of apportionment, binding on the States in every constitutional sense. The States have no right to question the propriety of the demand, and no discretion beyond devising the ways and means of furnishing the sums demanded. But although this is strictly and truly the case, and although the assumption of such a right would be an infringement of the articles of Union, and although it may seldom or never have been openly claimed, in practice the right has been constantly exercised, and would continue to be, as long as the revenues of the Confederacy remain dependent on the intermediate agency of its members. What the consequences of this system have been is known to every man the least familiar with our public affairs, and has been fully shown in different parts of these inquiries. It is this system that has contributed most to reduce us to a situation that gives ample cause both for mortification to ourselves and for triumph to our enemies.

What remedy can there be for this situation, except a change of the system that produced it, a change of the false and deceptive system of quotas and requisitions? What substitute can be imagined for this ignis fatuus in finance, other than permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by the ordinary methods of taxation authorized in every well-ordered constitution of civil government? Ingenious men may argue plausibly on any subject, but no human ingenuity can point out any other expedient to rescue us from the problems and embarrassments that naturally result from an inadequately supplied public treasury.

The more intelligent opponents of the new Constitution admit the force of this reasoning, but they qualify their admission with a distinction between what they call INTERNAL and EXTERNAL taxation. The former they would reserve to the State governments. The latter, which they explain as commercial imposts, or rather duties on imported articles, they declare themselves willing to concede to the federal head. This distinction, however, would violate the maxim of good sense and sound policy that every POWER ought to be in proportion to its OBJECT. It would also leave the general government in a kind of tutelage to the State governments, which is inconsistent with every idea of vigor or effectiveness. Who can pretend that commercial imposts are, or would be, alone equal to the present and future necessities of the Union? Take into account the existing debt, foreign and domestic, under any plan of paying it off that a man moderately impressed with the importance of public justice and public credit could approve, and add the establishments that all parties will acknowledge to be necessary. We could not reasonably flatter ourselves that this resource alone, even on the most improved scale, would suffice for our present necessities. Our future necessities admit of no calculation or limit, and on the principle I have more than once mentioned, the power of providing for them as they arise ought to be equally unconfined. I believe it may be regarded as a position warranted by the history of mankind that, IN THE USUAL PROGRESS OF THINGS, THE NECESSITIES OF A NATION, IN EVERY STAGE OF ITS EXISTENCE, WILL BE FOUND AT LEAST EQUAL TO ITS RESOURCES.

To say that shortfalls may be made up by requisitions upon the States is, on the one hand, to acknowledge that this system cannot be depended upon, and, on the other hand, to depend upon it for everything beyond a certain limit. Those who have carefully studied its vices and deformities, as experience has displayed them or as these papers have described them, must feel an invincible repugnance to trusting the national interests to its operation in any degree. Whenever it is put into action, its inevitable tendency must be to weaken the Union and to sow the seeds of discord and contention between the federal head and its members, and among the members themselves. Can it be expected that shortfalls would be better supplied in this way than the total wants of the Union have so far been supplied in the same way? It should be remembered that if less is required from the States, they will have proportionally less means to meet the demand. If the opinions of those who contend for the distinction I have mentioned were accepted as evidence of truth, one would be led to conclude that there was some known point in the economy of national affairs at which it would be safe to stop and say: Thus far the ends of public happiness will be advanced by supplying the wants of government, and all beyond this is unworthy of our care or anxiety. How is it possible for a government that is half supplied and always in need to fulfill the purposes of its institution, to provide for the security, advance the prosperity, or support the reputation of the commonwealth? How can it ever possess either energy or stability, dignity or credit, confidence at home or respectability abroad? How can its administration be anything other than a succession of expedients, temporizing, impotent and disgraceful? How will it be able to avoid frequently sacrificing its engagements to immediate necessity? How can it undertake or carry out any liberal or large-scale plans for the public good?

Let us consider what the effects of this situation would be in the very first war in which we happened to be engaged. We will suppose, for the sake of argument, that the revenue from the impost duties is enough to provide for the public debt and for a peacetime establishment for the Union. With things so arranged, a war breaks out. What would the government probably do in such an emergency? It has learned from experience that no proper dependence can be placed on the success of requisitions. It is unable, by its own authority, to lay hold of fresh resources. It is urged on by the danger to the nation. Would it not be driven to the expedient of diverting the funds already appropriated from their proper objects to the defense of the State? It is not easy to see how a step of this kind could be avoided; and if it were taken, it is evident that it would destroy public credit at the very moment when credit was becoming essential to the public safety. To imagine that credit might be dispensed with at such a crisis would be the height of infatuation. In the modern system of war, even the wealthiest nations are obliged to have recourse to large loans. A country so little wealthy as ours must feel this necessity much more strongly. But who would lend to a government that opened its overtures for borrowing with an act showing that no reliance could be placed on the steadiness of its measures for paying? The loans it might be able to obtain would be as limited in amount as they were burdensome in their conditions. They would be made on the same principles on which usurers commonly lend to bankrupt and fraudulent debtors: with a sparing hand and at enormous premiums.

It may perhaps be imagined that, because the resources of the country are scanty, the necessity of diverting the established funds in the case I have supposed would exist even if the national government possessed an unrestrained power of taxation. But two considerations should quiet all apprehension on this point. One is that we can be sure the resources of the community, in their full extent, will be brought into use for the benefit of the Union. The other is that whatever shortfalls there may be can be supplied without difficulty by loans.

The power to create new funds, from new objects of taxation, by its own authority, would enable the national government to borrow as far as its necessities might require. Foreigners, as well as the citizens of America, could then reasonably place confidence in its engagements. But to rely on a government that must itself depend on thirteen other governments for the means of fulfilling its contracts would, once its situation is clearly understood, require a degree of credulity not often met with in the money dealings of mankind, and one hardly reconcilable with the usual sharp-sightedness of avarice.

Reflections of this kind may carry little weight with men who hope to see the halcyon scenes of the poetic or fabulous age realized in America. But to those who believe we are likely to experience a common share of the ups and downs and calamities that have fallen to the lot of other nations, they must appear to deserve serious attention. Such men must view the actual situation of their country with painful concern, and must dread the evils that ambition or revenge might all too easily inflict upon it.
